questions.q: You are new to all of this and have no paid AI plan. Which assistant setup does the lesson suggest you start with?
options: Pay for Claude Code and Codex so you can compare them
GitHub Copilot Free inside VS Code
No assistant until you finish module 3
Any assistant you find in a video tutorial
questions.why: Copilot Free inside VS Code costs nothing and needs no terminal install, so it is the gentlest start.

questions.q: Why does the toolkit include Node.js when most labs use Python?
options: Python scripts cannot run without Node.js
VS Code is written in Node.js and needs it to open
Git uses Node.js to push to GitHub
Some AI tools install through npm, which comes with Node.js
questions.why: Node.js is needed mainly because some AI tools install through npm, its package manager.

questions.q: A friend says a coding assistant is just a chat app inside the editor. What is the key difference the lesson points out?
options: A coding assistant can read and edit files in the open folder and run terminal commands
A coding assistant only works offline
A chat app can run commands but a coding assistant cannot
There is no real difference, only the screen layout
questions.why: A chat app only sees what you paste, while a coding assistant can read files, edit them and run commands.

questions.q: You want to practice building a small budget report script this week. Which data should you use?
options: Your employer's real budget file, since it is realistic
A client file, as long as you delete it afterwards
Sample data you made up yourself
Real data, but only with a personal AI subscription
questions.why: The lesson says never use real work or client files for practice; make up your own sample data.

questions.q: You made three commits on a train with no internet. Where are those commits now?
options: On GitHub, because commits upload automatically
Lost, because Git needs internet to commit
In a staging area waiting to be committed
On your machine only, until you push
questions.why: A commit saves a snapshot locally; push is what sends commits to GitHub.

questions.q: Your commits show up on GitHub but not as yours on your profile. What is the most likely cause?
options: You did not turn on two-factor authentication
The email in git config does not match your GitHub account email
You used git add before git commit
Your repository is private
questions.why: Commits are linked to your profile by the email in git config, so a different email breaks that link.

questions.q: You turn on 2FA and GitHub shows recovery codes. What should you do with them?
options: Store them somewhere safe such as a password manager
Skip them, since the authenticator app is enough
Commit them to your journal so you never lose them
Paste them into your AI assistant for safe keeping
questions.why: Recovery codes let you back in if you lose your phone, so they must be saved somewhere safe and private.

questions.q: A repository already exists on GitHub and you want it on your laptop for the first time. Which command fits?
options: git init
git push
git clone
git add
questions.why: git clone copies a whole existing repository from GitHub to your machine the first time.

questions.q: You just installed Python, but the terminal says python3 is not found. What should you try first?
options: Reinstall VS Code
Open a new terminal so it picks up the updated PATH
Create a virtual environment
Install the Python extension from any publisher
questions.why: A terminal opened before the install does not see the new PATH, so a new terminal usually fixes it.

questions.q: Upgrading a package for project A broke project B on your laptop. What habit from the lesson would have prevented this?
options: Opening single files instead of folders
Committing the .venv folder to Git
Using one shared global Python for all projects
Giving each project its own virtual environment
questions.why: A virtual environment keeps each project's packages separate, so one upgrade cannot break another project.

questions.q: A client asks you to look at a broken report script while they watch. How should you open it in VS Code?
options: Open the project folder, then use the integrated terminal from there
Open just the one script file by double clicking it
Open your whole home folder so nothing is missing
Copy the script into a chat app and run it there
questions.why: Opening a folder lets the terminal, Git and assistants work properly, and the terminal starts in that folder.

questions.q: You search the Extensions view for Python and see several results with similar names. What should you check before installing?
options: Which one has the newest icon
Which one is listed first
The publisher name, which should be Microsoft
Nothing, all extensions are reviewed and safe
questions.why: Copycat extensions exist, so you confirm the publisher before installing.

questions.q: You start a coding assistant for the first time in your learning folder. What kind of task should you give it first?
options: Refactor every file in the folder
Install all the packages it thinks you need
Commit and push your work for you
A read-only task, such as explaining what is in the folder
questions.why: A read-only task cannot break anything, so it is a safe way to see how the tool behaves.

questions.q: The assistant asks to run a command you do not understand. What should you do?
options: Approve it, since the tool sounds confident
Say no or ask it to explain why the command is needed
Switch to the least careful approval setting so it stops asking
Run it yourself in a different terminal instead
questions.why: If you would not run the command yourself, you say no and ask why; confidence is not correctness.

questions.q: In Claude Code, what does Plan mode do?
options: Describes what it will do and waits for your approval before changing anything
Runs all edits automatically and shows a summary afterwards
Picks the cheapest model for the task
Pushes your changes to GitHub on a schedule
questions.why: Plan mode lays out the intended actions and waits for your approval before changing files.

questions.q: A video shows a one-line command to install Codex. Where should you take the install command from?
options: The video, if it has many views
A forum post that says the command worked
The official docs or README for the tool
Whatever command your AI chat app suggests
questions.why: Install commands should come only from the official docs, not random blogs or videos.

questions.q: In a daily journal entry, which section does the lesson call the most valuable?
options: Links
Questions I still have
What I learned
What broke and how I fixed it
questions.why: The error, what you tried and what worked is real debugging evidence for a reviewer.

questions.q: You recorded a 4 minute walkthrough of a lab. How should it go into your journal?
options: Upload it somewhere you control and paste the link in that week's entry
Commit the video file into the labs folder
Convert it to text and commit the transcript only
Skip it, videos do not belong in a journal
questions.why: Git is built for text, not large videos, so you link to the video instead of committing it.

questions.q: Your journal repository is public. A lab at work went well and you want to note it. What is the right move?
options: Add the client name so it looks more impressive
Paste the real data you used so others can reproduce it
Leave out any employer or client information
Make it private for a day, add the details, then make it public
questions.why: Never put employer or client information in the journal; anything public should be treated as public forever.

questions.q: You plan to write all your journal entries on Sunday. Why does the lesson advise against that?
options: GitHub only accepts one commit per day
Small daily commits show steady progress and are easier to write
Weekend commits are hidden on your profile
Git cannot track files edited more than once a week
questions.why: Daily commits give a dated record of steady progress and keep each entry short and fresh.
